title: Guha, Rama's friend
hookLine: at the edge of the kingdom, on the bank of the Ganga, a forest king runs to meet his friend
carry: sakhya: loving God as a friend
tomorrow: The night watch on the Ganga

cards: The chariot crosses river after river, through villages already talking about the prince who's been sent away.
At the southern edge of the kingdom of Kosala, Rama turns in the chariot, faces the way they've come, and says goodbye to Ayodhya and its gods. Then they ride on to the Ganga.
Near a town called Shringaverapura the river is wide and bright. And on its bank lives someone who has heard Rama is coming.

teach.b: His name is Guha, king of the Nishadas, a people who live by the forest and the river, hunting, fishing and running boats.

teach.h: A FRIEND AS DEAR AS LIFE.
teach.b: Valmiki introduces him with one phrase: Rama's friend, as dear to him as his own life. Guha comes out with his family, carrying food and drink of every kind.
Rama sees him from a distance, and before Guha can bow, Rama embraces him. Then Guha makes an extraordinary offer. This land is yours, as Ayodhya is.
Stay. Rule here. Rama thanks him warmly and says no.
He has vowed to live fourteen years as a forest ascetic, and he won't break it on his first day.

He accepts one thing, and it's not for himself: please feed the horses; they're my father's, and he loves them. That night Guha and Lakshmana sit up by the fire, bows in hand, while Rama and Sita sleep on the ground.
Hindus have a name for Guha's kind of love.
The Bhagavata Purana lists nine forms of bhakti, nine ways of loving God, and one of them is sakhya: friendship.

teach.h: AN EMBRACE AND THE WORD FRIEND.
teach.b: You can love God as a servant loves a master, or a child a parent; you can also love God as a friend, with no fear and no ceremony, just food carried down to the river.
Devotional retellings treasure this scene for a second reason: Guha is a forest king, outside the royal world, and Rama's embrace doesn't ask who his family was. It just says friend.

how: Many Hindus honor Guha as a model of devoted friendship; Shringaverapura, near Prayagraj, is visited by pilgrims as the place where Rama met him.

o: a sage who hosts Rama at the meeting of rivers
the ferryman who demands payment to cross the river
the Nishada king who welcomes Rama as a dear friend

games.q: the friend on the river — tap the pairs.
p: the only thing Rama asks Guha to feed

s: Rama and Guha meet for the first time at the Ganga
Valmiki calls Guha his old friend, as dear as his own life.
Rama thanks him and declines, keeping his vow.
in Hinduism, you can only approach God as a servant
friendship, sakhya, is one of the nine forms of bhakti. Guha is its picture.

games.q: your nani chats with God like an old friend. your cousin says that isn't 'real' prayer. by Guha and Rama, what fits?
o: it's real bhakti: sakhya, loving God as a friend.
real prayer has to be formal and in sanskrit.
only priests should talk to God directly.
games.why: friendship, sakhya, is one of the nine forms of bhakti, and Rama answers Guha's love with an embrace and the word friend.

practice: Many Hindus talk to God plainly, like a friend, at the home shrine or anywhere. If you pray, tell God one ordinary thing about your day, out loud or silently, the way Guha would have talked by the fire.
If you don't, picture a friend who showed up for you when things were bad, and breathe out thanks.

wordCard.voice: Guha, king of the Nishadas on the Ganga, Rama's friend as dear as his own life: a picture of sakhya, loving God as a friend.

orig.note: Sanskrit niṣāda: the name for Guha's people, forest and river dwellers who hunt, fish and run boats.

carryVoice: Your line: sakhya: loving God as a friend. Guha's watch has only begun. Day five hundred thirty-four.
